sentences.text: A compass holds a small magnet balanced so it can swing.
That magnet is often shaped as a needle, and one end is the north-seeking end.
Earth acts like a giant, slightly uneven magnet, with a magnetic field around it.
The needle lines up with that field.
The north-seeking end points toward magnetic north, not toward the biggest piece of metal nearby.
Magnetic north is close to the geographic North Pole, but it is not the exact same spot.
The difference between those two norths is called declination, and it changes from place to place.
A hiker who needs a precise path has to account for that difference.
A compass can be pulled off course by nearby iron, or by a magnet in a phone case, because those tug on the needle too.
A careful user steps away from cars, metal fences, and electronics before trusting the reading.
Polaris, the North Star, is a different clue. It is a star, not a magnet, and it helps only when the northern sky is visible.
A compass can work in fog, under clouds, and during the day, which is why travelers still carry one.
Using it well means holding it level, letting the needle settle, and then matching your map or your body to the reading.
The needle does not decide the destination. It only shows a direction so a person can choose.
If the needle jitters and will not settle, something nearby is probably tugging it, and the reading is not ready.

questions.prompt: What is this passage mostly about?

choices.text: How a compass needle shows direction, and what can fool it
How to turn a phone into the North Star
Why magnetic north is a kind of star
How hikers move the geographic North Pole

questions.explanation: The passage explains the magnetic needle, the difference between two norths, and the nearby metal that can spoil a reading. That is the main idea.

choices.text: The shine of the North Star
The difference between magnetic north and the geographic North Pole
The weight of a compass needle
The fog that hides a trail

questions.explanation: The passage defines declination as the difference between magnetic north and the geographic North Pole, and says it changes from place to place.

questions.prompt: The needle needs to settle. What does settle mean here?

choices.text: To point at the brightest star
To melt into the map
To stop swinging and hold still
To grow louder in the fog

questions.explanation: Settle, in this passage, means to stop moving and hold still. A jittery needle has not settled, so the reading is not ready.

questions.prompt: The needle keeps swinging beside a metal fence. What should the hiker figure out?

choices.text: The fence has become the North Star
Declination disappears near any fence
A swinging needle is the most accurate reading
The fence may be tugging the needle, so this is a poor place to read it

questions.explanation: The passage says iron can tug the needle and that a needle which will not settle is being pulled by something nearby. The fence is a strong clue.

questions.prompt: Which order fits a careful compass reading?

choices.text: Step away from iron, hold the compass level, let the needle settle, then choose a direction
Choose a direction, then stand beside a car, then shake the needle
Look only at Polaris, then ignore the needle in clear weather
Let the needle jitter, then trust it at once

questions.explanation: The passage tells a careful user to leave cars and fences first, hold the compass level, wait for the needle to settle, and only then use the direction.
